name: Hart v. City of Grand Rapids
court: Sixth Circuit (from the Western District of Michigan)
citation: 138 F.4th 409 (6th Cir. 2025), cert. denied sub nom. Reinink v. Hart, No. 25-179 (U.S. May 26, 2026)
topic: Crowd control munitions at a protest; pointing a launcher, pepper spray, and a long range chemical munition fired at a person at close range treated as deadly force; qualified immunity; municipal ratification
summary: During a 2020 Grand Rapids demonstration that had turned violent, officers pointed a 40 millimeter launcher at a car's passenger, pepper sprayed a man who walked toward the police line, and then fired a long range tear gas canister directly into his shoulder from a few feet away as he turned back after retreating. The Sixth Circuit granted qualified immunity to the first two officers because no case clearly established those uses of force were unlawful, but denied it to the officer who fired the canister, holding that the munition fired at that range was deadly force and that it was clearly established that deadly force may not be used on an unarmed person who poses no immediate threat, even in a riot. Judge Larsen dissented in part. The Supreme Court denied certiorari, with two Justices voting to summarily reverse. It is taught for the rule that the nature of the force, not the label on the weapon, decides the standard.

facts:
The facts are as the Sixth Circuit stated them, largely undisputed and captured on bystander video, viewed in the plaintiffs' favor on review of summary judgment. On May 30, 2020, a racial justice demonstration in downtown Grand Rapids, Michigan, had become what the district court called complete mayhem. Beginning around 7:45 p.m. some demonstrators surrounded officers and threw rocks, bricks, and bottles with unknown substances; there was property damage and escalating violence. Officers broadcast dispersal orders warning that failure to disperse could result in arrest or the use of chemical agents or less than lethal munitions.

The department's Special Response Team carried crowd control packs with two 40 millimeter munitions whose cartridges look similar: Muzzle Blast, a powder dispersion round designed to be fired at individuals at close range, and Spede-Heat, a tear gas canister designed to be launched into an area at long range and not directly at a person. Department witnesses testified that Spede-Heat's muzzle velocity requires firing it into the air at a 45 to 60 degree angle, that firing it directly at a person would absolutely be lethal force except in a life or death situation, and that firing it at a person at close distance is considered potential deadly force.

Around 11:40 p.m., Sean Hart and Tiffany Guzman drove to an intersection near a police line that had been cleared and sat there playing an anti police song loudly. Three officers, concerned the car might drive into the line, approached. Officer Benjamin Johnson held his launcher, loaded with Muzzle Blast, at the high ready pointed toward the passenger side where Guzman sat, and ordered them to leave. They did.

Less than two minutes later they returned. Hart parked about 50 feet from the line, got out leaving his door open, and walked toward the officers with his left hand in his pocket. Officers yelled at him to get back. Hart stopped several feet from the line, withdrew his hand, and pointed at the officers; he was unarmed and held a cigarette in his right hand. Sergeant Brad Bush stepped forward and pepper sprayed Hart's head for two to three seconds from eight to ten feet. Hart turned, took a few steps away, lifted his head, took a drag from his cigarette, and began turning back toward the line. Officer Phillip Reinink left the line after the spraying began and, as Hart was turning back a few feet away, fired a Spede-Heat canister that struck Hart's left shoulder. Reinink testified he believed he had loaded Muzzle Blast; he had loaded the munition without a witness, contrary to policy, and his body camera was off. Hart stayed on his feet, gestured at the officers, and walked back to his car. He later drove slowly toward the officers, revved his engine, and left. Hart was treated for shoulder pain, abrasion, and bruising and for eye irritation. Guzman was not physically injured.

The department sustained an excessive force finding against Reinink and found he violated procedures on loading munitions and on body camera use; he received two days of unpaid leave. Hart and Guzman sued the three officers and the city under 42 U.S.C. section 1983. The district court granted summary judgment to all defendants.
holding:
Affirmed as to Officer Johnson, Sergeant Bush, and the city; reversed as to Officer Reinink and remanded. Judge Stranch wrote for the court, joined by Judge Gilman; Judge Larsen concurred as to Johnson, Bush, and the city and dissented as to Reinink.

Separate analysis. The court analyzed each officer's use of force separately, quoting Plakas v. Drinski for the practice of carving the incident into segments and judging each on its own terms, and considered each officer's entitlement to qualified immunity separately.

Officer Johnson. Pointing a launcher loaded with Muzzle Blast at the passenger window did not violate clearly established law. The cases Guzman relied on involved officers holding compliant occupants of a home at gunpoint with actual firearms during a lengthy search, or pointing a gun at the head of an unarmed man leaving his home. Here the encounter was in a public street during an ongoing disorderly demonstration, the occupants appeared to ignore dispersal orders by driving toward the line, the encounter lasted a couple of minutes, and the launcher carried a non lethal chemical round.

Sergeant Bush. Pepper spraying Hart did not violate clearly established law. The cases Hart cited involved a person not actively resisting, a person passively awaiting police who was sprayed at such close range that he collapsed unconscious, and a person walking slowly toward an officer with his hands above his head during a riot. Hart, by contrast, had returned to the scene after being ordered away, got out of his car, and advanced toward the line in defiance of orders. None of those cases put the unlawfulness of the spray beyond debate.

Officer Reinink: deadly force. The court first held that firing Spede-Heat directly at a person a few feet away must be analyzed as deadly force. Reinink admitted he was trained that some uses of Spede-Heat could cause serious injury or death and that it could be considered a deadly weapon; the SRT commander and the chief said firing it at a person at that distance would be lethal or potentially deadly force. Reinink's claimed intent to fire Muzzle Blast was irrelevant under Graham, which makes intent immaterial. "Though deadly force precedent centers on firearms, the reasoning of these cases clarifies that it is the nature of the force, not the weapon, that matters."

Officer Reinink: constitutional violation. Deadly force is unreasonable unless the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses an imminent threat of serious physical harm. Applying the Sixth Circuit's Palma factors, the court found the tumultuous scene weighed for Reinink and the brief interval between Hart's turn and the shot weighed for him, but that Hart was visibly unarmed with his hands withdrawn from his pocket, had not verbally or physically threatened the officers, had stopped advancing and retreated after being sprayed, was eight to ten feet away, and that Reinink's own intent to use Muzzle Blast showed a less forceful option was available. The court also said Reinink's policy violations, loading without a witness and operating without a body camera, do not by themselves defeat qualified immunity but are relevant to the first prong, and that a jury could find his conduct plainly incompetent rather than a reasonable split second judgment. A reasonable jury could find excessive force.

Officer Reinink: clearly established. It has been settled for a generation that deadly force may not be used where the suspect poses no immediate threat to the officer or others (Garner). Sample v. Bailey held deadly force impermissible against a suspect whose movement was limited, who was not verbally threatening, and whose hands were visible and empty. Ciminillo v. Streicher held that less than deadly force against an individual displaying no aggression in a riot is not reasonable; the court said that if a hazy border existed about some degree of nonlethal force in a riot, it was beyond debate that deadly force may not be used against a person displaying no aggression. The court rejected the dissent's distinctions, saying an unarmed man is not displaying aggressive behavior by keeping his arms at his sides or turning around in place.

The city. The plaintiffs preserved only a ratification theory, which requires a clear and persistent pattern of inadequate investigations of comparable claims. Their spreadsheet of about 90 excessive force complaints from 2015 to 2020, nearly all not sustained, listed only the allegation and the finding with no substantive description of the events or the investigations, which was insufficient without qualitative specifics. Any failure to train claim was abandoned.

The Supreme Court. Reinink's petition for certiorari was denied on May 26, 2026. Justices Thomas and Alito would have granted the petition and summarily reversed for essentially the reasons given in Judge Larsen's separate opinion.
notDecided:
Whether Officer Reinink actually used excessive force. The court held that a reasonable jury could so find on the facts viewed in Hart's favor and remanded; it did not find liability.

Whether Officer Johnson's and Sergeant Bush's uses of force were reasonable. The court decided those claims on the clearly established prong only.

Whether the city could be liable on a failure to train theory. The court held that theory abandoned because it was not argued to the district court or connected to record evidence on appeal.

The state law claims, which the district court dismissed without prejudice after declining supplemental jurisdiction.

The denial of certiorari is not a ruling on the merits by the Supreme Court. Two Justices recorded their disagreement with the Sixth Circuit; the Court as a whole expressed no view.
inPractice:
Hart matters most for one sentence: it is the nature of the force, not the weapon, that matters. Officers tend to classify tools by their label. The Sixth Circuit classified the use. A tear gas canister designed to be lobbed into an area at long range, fired directly into a person's shoulder from a few feet away, was analyzed as deadly force, because the department's own trainers said that is what it was at that range. The officer's belief that he had loaded a different round did not matter; Graham makes intent irrelevant.

The second lesson is about the two officers who received immunity. Pointing a launcher at a car that had ignored dispersal orders in a violent crowd, and pepper spraying a man who returned after being told to leave and walked at the police line with his hand in his pocket, were not clearly unlawful on the cases the plaintiffs cited. The court did not say those uses of force were reasonable. It said no prior case put their unlawfulness beyond debate in a riot setting where the person was defying orders and advancing.

The third lesson is about what changed between the spray and the shot. The court's analysis of Reinink turned on the moments after the pepper spray: Hart had turned away, stepped back, was visibly unarmed, and was eight to ten feet off when he began to turn around. The dissent read the same video as a man undeterred by pepper spray, angry, turning back toward officers. Reasonable judges disagreed, and two Supreme Court Justices sided with the dissent. The lesson for officers is not to count on that disagreement.

Dr. Sowards teaches Hart in the less lethal line with Deorle, Bryan v. MacPherson, and Headwaters, and in the impact weapons course for the principle that specialty munitions have manufacturer and department limits that define the level of force. The court also treated the officer's policy violations, loading without a witness and an inactive body camera, as relevant to whether his conduct was competent. Equipment discipline is force discipline.
trainIt:
Teach munitions by their deployment envelope, not their name. Hart turned on the difference between a close range dispersion round and a long range canister fired through the same launcher with similar looking cartridges. Instructors should require students to state, for each specialty munition they carry, the minimum range, the target area, the intended deployment, and what the use becomes if those limits are violated. The Sixth Circuit accepted the department's own testimony that a long range canister fired at a person at close range is deadly force. That testimony came from the officer, the SRT commander, and the chief.

Teach the loading protocol as a force safeguard. Reinink loaded the munition without a witness, in violation of policy, and the court treated that violation and his inactive body camera as relevant to whether a jury could find his conduct plainly incompetent. Train the witness verification step as the control that prevents exactly this mistake, and teach that policy violations in the preparation phase can follow the officer into the courtroom.

Teach reassessment after a less lethal application. Run the sequence: subject advances, pepper spray applied, subject turns away and retreats, subject begins to turn back. Ask students what they see and what the threat is at the moment of turning back. The majority saw an unarmed man, hands at his sides, not advancing. The dissent saw an angry man undeterred by spray. Students should learn to articulate specific threat indicators, a weapon, a movement toward officers, a verbal threat, rather than relying on the chaos of the scene alone, which the court treated as the only factor favoring the officer.

Teach the clearly established lesson from Johnson and Bush honestly. Both received immunity because the law was not specific enough for a riot setting, not because the court approved what they did. Immunity decisions should not be taught as tactical endorsements.
caution: The Sixth Circuit opinion is published and precedential in the Sixth Circuit; it was read in full from govinfo. Certiorari was denied on May 26, 2026, which is not a Supreme Court ruling on the merits; Justices Thomas and Alito would have summarily reversed for the reasons in Judge Larsen's partial dissent. The court held only that a jury could find Officer Reinink used excessive force and that the law was clearly established; no liability finding has been made. The grants of qualified immunity to Officer Johnson and Sergeant Bush rest on the clearly established prong and are not findings that their force was reasonable. The brief uses the Sixth Circuit's Palma factors and Ciminillo precedent, which are Sixth Circuit law and not binding in the Ninth Circuit.
dissent: Judge Larsen concurred as to Officer Johnson, Sergeant Bush, and the city, and dissented as to Officer Reinink. She would have granted him qualified immunity because Hart failed to carry his burden of identifying a case that would have told a reasonable officer his specific conduct was unlawful. Hart relied on a single case, Ciminillo, which was not a lethal force case and which involved a man walking toward officers with both hands raised in surrender while trying to leave the riot. Hart, by contrast, returned to the scene despite orders to leave, advanced on the officers with a hand in his pocket, never raised his hands in surrender, pointed at the officers, was undeterred by pepper spray, and by his own testimony turned back because he was mad. She said the majority's additional cases were distinguishable: Sample involved a suspect found in a cabinet whose movement was limited, while Hart was eight to ten feet away and could charge at any moment; Lewis involved a fleeing suspect and was unpublished, and the majority used it only for a general proposition, which does not suffice in the excessive force context. She emphasized that specific cases are especially important in excessive force law and that it is the plaintiff's burden to produce one. At the Supreme Court, Justices Thomas and Alito would have granted certiorari and summarily reversed for essentially her reasons.

applications.title: The nature of the force, not the weapon
applications.body: A long range chemical canister fired directly at a person a few feet away was analyzed as deadly force because the department's own trainers said it would be. The label on the munition does not set the standard; the use does.

applications.title: Intent to use a different round is irrelevant
applications.body: Reinink believed he had loaded a close range dispersion round. Under Graham, an officer's good intentions do not make an objectively unreasonable use of force constitutional. Loading protocols exist to prevent this mistake.

applications.title: Deadly force on a non threatening person is clearly unlawful even in a riot
applications.body: The court held it was beyond debate that an officer may not use deadly force against an unarmed person displaying no aggression, even during a riot, where the person had retreated after pepper spray and was merely turning around.

applications.title: Immunity for the launcher and the spray was not approval
applications.body: Pointing a launcher at a car defying dispersal orders and pepper spraying a man advancing on the line were not clearly unlawful on the cases cited. The court did not decide whether they were reasonable.

applications.title: Preparation violations follow you
applications.body: Loading without a witness and an inactive body camera did not by themselves defeat immunity, but the court treated them as relevant to whether a jury could find the officer plainly incompetent rather than making a reasonable split second judgment.

quiz.q: Why did the Sixth Circuit analyze Officer Reinink's firing of the Spede-Heat canister as deadly force?
options: Because any 40 millimeter launcher is a deadly weapon
Because the munition was fired directly at a person at close range, and the officer, the SRT commander, and the chief all testified that use at that range is lethal or potentially deadly force
Because Reinink intended to kill Hart
quiz.teach: The court said it is the nature of the force, not the weapon, that matters, and that the officer's intent to fire a different round was irrelevant under Graham.

quiz.q: Why did Sergeant Bush receive qualified immunity for pepper spraying Hart?
options: Because the court held pepper spray can never be excessive force
Because none of the cases Hart cited placed beyond debate that spraying a man who returned after being ordered away and advanced toward the police line during a riot was unlawful
quiz.teach: The court distinguished cases involving people who were not resisting, who were passively waiting, or who approached with hands raised, and decided the claim on the clearly established prong without deciding whether the spray was reasonable.

quiz.q: What happened when Officer Reinink sought Supreme Court review?
options: The Court reversed the Sixth Circuit
The Court denied certiorari on May 26, 2026; Justices Thomas and Alito would have granted and summarily reversed for the reasons in Judge Larsen's partial dissent
The Court granted certiorari and set the case for argument
The Court vacated and remanded in light of Zorn v. Linton
quiz.teach: A denial of certiorari is not a merits ruling. The Sixth Circuit's decision stands, and the case returns to the district court for proceedings against Reinink.
